seo.shortDescription: Searchable duty table for all 556 HTS Chapter 44 lines: logs, softwood and hardwood lumber, OSB, MDF, plywood, mouldings, doors, flooring, pallets and wood charcoal. Base rates, the 10% Section 232 softwood lumber duty, the 2026 Section 301 duties, Section 338 on Canada, and the lumber and plywood AD/CVD cases.

overview.intro:
Chapter 44 covers wood and articles of wood: fuel wood and pellets (4401), wood charcoal (4402), logs (4403), sawn lumber (4407), veneer (4408), mouldings and flooring strips (4409), particle board and OSB (4410), fiberboard and MDF (4411), plywood (4412), frames, pallets, barrels, tools, builders' joinery such as doors, windows and engineered flooring (4418), kitchenware (4419), ornaments (4420) and other wooden articles (4421). The U.S. imported **$23.21B** of these goods in 2025, 44% from Canada. Most lines are **Free** at base; **200 of 556** lines carry a base rate, mostly 3.2% to 8% on plywood, joinery and wooden articles.

Since **October 14, 2025**, softwood timber and lumber (15 provisions in 4403, 4406 and 4407.11–4407.19) pay a **10% Section 232 duty** from every country, including Canada and Mexico with a USMCA claim; for those lines it replaces the 2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties. Canadian softwood lumber also pays **antidumping and countervailing duties** (35.16% combined for most exporters), so it carries about 45% in all. Most other lines pay the **2026 Section 301 duty** of 10% or 12.5% from the 60 listed economies (tropical woods are exempt), **Brazil** adds 25%, **China** pays 25% under List 3 (7.5% for 11 List 4A lines) plus 12.5%, and **154 Canadian** lines, including most plywood, MDF, mouldings and doors, pay **50% under Section 338** since August 22, 2026, even with a USMCA claim. Hardwood plywood is also under AD/CVD orders on China and new cases on China, Indonesia and Vietnam. Wooden kitchen cabinets, vanities and upholstered furniture fall in Chapter 94, not here.

stats.label: Lines with an extra duty for some origins
stats.note: 2026 Section 301: 525 (tropical woods exempt; softwood lumber pays Section 232 instead); China List 3 or 4A: 529; Brazil 25%: 456; Section 338 on Canada: 154; Section 232 softwood: 106; Russia 35%: 144. USMCA goods are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty only.

productGroups.label: Fuel wood, wood chips, sawdust & wood pellets
productGroups.blurb: Fuel wood, wood chips, sawdust and wood waste, and pellets or briquettes of it: 13 lines, all Free. They pay the 10% or 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty from the 60 listed economies (USMCA goods exempt); Canadian nonconiferous fuel wood (4401.12) pays 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Wood charcoal, incl. shell & bamboo charcoal
productGroups.blurb: Wood charcoal, including bamboo and coconut-shell charcoal, agglomerated or not: 3 lines, all Free. Lump and briquette charcoal of 4402.90 from Canada pays 50% under Section 338; activated charcoal is heading 3802, not here.

productGroups.label: Logs and wood in the rough
productGroups.blurb: Logs and roughly squared wood, by species: 85 lines, all Free. Coniferous logs (4403.11, 4403.21–4403.26) and 4403.99 pay the 10% Section 232 duty; teak and other tropical logs and eucalyptus logs are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.

productGroups.label: Hoopwood, split poles, stakes & sticks
productGroups.blurb: Hoopwood, split poles, pointed stakes and roughly trimmed sticks: 6 lines, all Free. Only the 2026 Section 301, Brazil and China duties reach them.

productGroups.label: Wood wool (excelsior) & wood flour
productGroups.blurb: Wood wool (excelsior) and wood flour: one line at 3.2%.

productGroups.label: Railway sleepers (cross-ties)
productGroups.blurb: Wooden railway and tramway sleepers (cross-ties): 4 lines, all Free. Coniferous ties (4406.11, 4406.91) pay the 10% Section 232 duty.

productGroups.label: Sawn lumber: softwood, hardwood & tropical
productGroups.blurb: Wood sawn or chipped lengthwise, over 6 mm thick: 74 lines, all Free. Softwood lumber (4407.11 pine, 4407.12 fir and spruce, 4407.13 S-P-F, 4407.14 hem-fir, 4407.19 other) pays the 10% Section 232 duty from every country, and Canadian softwood lumber also pays AD/CVD. Hardwood lumber pays the 2026 Section 301 duty; tropical lumber is exempt.

productGroups.label: Veneer sheets
productGroups.blurb: Veneer and sheets for plywood, up to 6 mm thick: 27 lines, all Free. Tropical veneer (4408.31, 4408.39) is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; Canadian coniferous veneer (4408.10) pays 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Mouldings, flooring strips & continuously shaped wood
productGroups.blurb: Wood continuously shaped along an edge or face: mouldings, tongue-and-groove boards, unassembled flooring strips: 47 lines, Free to 4.9%. Wood mouldings and millwork from China are under AD/CVD orders, and several Canadian coniferous moulding lines pay 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Particle board & OSB
productGroups.blurb: Particle board, oriented strand board (OSB) and waferboard: 11 lines, all Free. Canadian OSB is Free with a USMCA claim; Canadian "other" board of 4410.19 pays 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Fiberboard & MDF
productGroups.blurb: Fiberboard of wood, including MDF and hardboard: 36 lines, Free to 6% (some at 1.9¢/kg + 1.5%). Composite panels must meet EPA's TSCA Title VI formaldehyde limits; Canadian MDF over 5 mm pays 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Plywood, LVL & veneered panels
productGroups.blurb: Plywood, veneered panels, LVL and blockboard: 123 lines, Free to 8%. The group with the most trade remedies: AD/CVD orders on hardwood plywood from China (and Chinese-core plywood finished in Vietnam), new final determinations on China, Indonesia and Vietnam, and 50% Section 338 on most Canadian plywood.

productGroups.label: Densified wood
productGroups.blurb: Densified wood in blocks, plates, strips or profiles: one line at 3.7%. From Canada it pays 50% under Section 338 (9903.03.12).

productGroups.label: Wooden picture & mirror frames
productGroups.blurb: Wooden frames for paintings, photographs and mirrors: 2 lines at 3.9%.

productGroups.label: Pallets, crates, boxes & cable drums
productGroups.blurb: Packing cases, boxes, crates, cable drums, pallets and pallet collars: 5 lines, Free or 10.7%. Wood packaging used to ship any goods must be ISPM 15 treated and marked.

productGroups.label: Barrels, casks & staves
productGroups.blurb: Casks, barrels, vats, tubs and staves: 10 lines, Free or 3.2%.

productGroups.label: Tools, tool handles & shoe lasts
productGroups.blurb: Wooden tools, tool bodies and handles, broom and brush bodies and handles, and shoe lasts and trees: 5 lines, Free or 5.1%.

productGroups.label: Builders' joinery: doors, windows, flooring, glulam
productGroups.blurb: Builders' joinery and carpentry: windows, doors, formwork, shingles and shakes, posts and beams, glulam, CLT, I-joists and assembled flooring panels: 45 lines, Free to 8%. Multilayered wood flooring from China is under AD/CVD orders, and Canadian wooden doors pay 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Wooden tableware & kitchenware
productGroups.blurb: Wooden tableware and kitchenware such as cutting boards, chopsticks, bowls and utensils: 8 lines, 3.2% or 5.3%. Wooden handicrafts from China must be treated and tagged under APHIS rules.

productGroups.label: Wood marquetry, jewelry boxes & ornaments
productGroups.blurb: Marquetry and inlaid wood, jewelry and cutlery boxes, statuettes and ornaments, and small wooden furniture not in Chapter 94: 8 lines, Free to 4.3%.

productGroups.label: Other articles of wood
productGroups.blurb: Other wooden articles: hangers, spools, toothpicks, skewers, dowels, edge-glued lumber, pickets, wooden blinds and more: 42 lines, Free to 10.7% or 6.5¢ per gross. Wood mouldings and millwork from China can enter here and stay under the AD/CVD orders.

rateTable.note: Rates shown in grey are inherited from the parent heading. HTSUS states a duty once on the 8-digit line and leaves the 10-digit statistical lines blank; this table resolves each line to the rate that actually applies to it.

workedExamples.title: $100,000 of S-P-F softwood lumber from Canada
workedExamples.body: Softwood lumber is **Free** at base. Since October 14, 2025 it pays the **10% Section 232 duty** (9903.76.01), with or without a USMCA claim: **$10,000**. It also pays the antidumping and countervailing duty cash deposits on softwood lumber from Canada. For the companies not individually examined in the latest completed reviews these are **20.53% AD** (90 FR 44035) and **14.63% CVD** (90 FR 38755): another **$35,160**, so about **$45,160** in all. Canfor (35.47% + 12.12%) and West Fraser (9.65% + 16.82%) have their own rates. The tariff calculator shows the 10% only.

workedExamples.title: $100,000 of hardwood-faced plywood from Vietnam
workedExamples.body: Plywood with a non-coniferous outer ply of 4412.33.32 has an **8%** base rate, and the 2026 Section 301 duty on Vietnam (9903.05.84) adds **12.5%**: **$20,500**. Hardwood and decorative plywood from Vietnam is also covered by Commerce's final AD (90.12%) and CVD (47.68% for most exporters) determinations of July 21, 2026, and the ITC found injury on September 9, 2026. The orders had not been published by October 13, 2026; once they are, cash deposits at those rates add **$137,800**. Plywood finished in Vietnam from Chinese veneers or cores is covered by the 2018 China orders.

workedExamples.title: MDF and OSB from Canada
workedExamples.body: MDF over 9 mm thick of 4411.14.90 has a **3.9%** base rate, which a USMCA claim removes. Since August 22, 2026 it is on the Section 338 list (U.S. note 51(b)(3), 9903.03.14), so Canadian MDF pays **50%** even with a USMCA claim, or 3.9% + 50% + 10% (2026 Section 301) = **63.9%** without one. Canadian OSB (4410.12) is not on the list: **Free** with USMCA, 10% without.

workedExamples.title: $10,000 of wooden articles from China
workedExamples.body: Other articles of wood of 4421.99.98 pay **3.3%** base, **25%** under Section 301 List 3 (9903.88.03) and **12.5%** under the 2026 Section 301 action (9903.05.31): **40.8%**, or **$4,080**. Wooden handicrafts over 1 cm in diameter from China must also be heat-treated or fumigated and tagged with the manufacturer's name under 7 CFR 319.40-5(o).

workedExamples.title: Spruce lumber from Germany or Sweden
workedExamples.body: European fir and spruce lumber is **Free** at base and pays the **10% Section 232 duty** (9903.76.01). Proclamation 10976 caps EU wood at 15% including the base rate, which a 10% duty on a Free line stays under. The EU's 10% 2026 Section 301 rate (9903.05.39) does not apply on top (U.S. note 52(f)), so the total is **10%**. EU hardwood lumber pays the 10% Section 301 rate instead.

**Note 3.** Headings 4414 to 4421 apply to articles of particle board, fiberboard, laminated wood or densified wood as they apply to articles of wood.

**Note 4.** Products of 4410, 4411 or 4412 may be shaped as in 4409, curved, corrugated, perforated or cut to non-rectangular shapes, provided this does not give them the character of articles of other headings.

**Note 6.** Subject to note 1, "wood" in a heading also covers bamboo and other woody materials.

**Subheading notes.** Wood pellets (4401.31) are cylindrical, up to 25 mm in diameter and 100 mm long, with no more than 3% binder; wood briquettes (4401.32) have a minimum cross-section over 25 mm. seo.shortDescription: What changed for U.S. lumber, plywood and wood product imports since January 2025: the 10% Section 232 softwood lumber duty, the IEEPA duties and their end, Section 122, the 2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties, Section 338 on Canada, and the softwood lumber and hardwood plywood AD/CVD cases, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). The base rates of all 555 lines that exist in both are unchanged; 4420.19.00 (other statuettes and ornaments, 3.2%) is new in the current edition.

The extra duties changed a lot. In 2025 the IEEPA tariffs reached wood in stages: non-USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico paid 25% (Canada 35% from August 1), Brazil paid 40%, and the reciprocal tariff hit wooden articles of 4414–4421, while logs, lumber, panels and plywood of 4401–4413 were exempt under Annex II pending the Section 232 timber investigation. On **October 14, 2025** the **Section 232** duty took effect: **10% on softwood timber and lumber** from every country, and the rest of Chapter 44 lost its reciprocal-tariff exemption. All IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026**; the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on **July 23, 2026**.

Today five measures apply: the **10% Section 232** duty on softwood, the **2026 Section 301 duties** on 60 economies (from July 24, 2026; tropical woods exempt), **Brazil's 25% Section 301 duty** (from July 22, 2026), **Section 338 at 50%** on 154 Canadian lines (from August 22, 2026), and China's Section 301 **List 3 and 4A** duties. Antidumping and countervailing duties on **softwood lumber from Canada**, **hardwood plywood**, **wood mouldings** and **multilayered wood flooring from China** are listed below for reference and are **not included in the tariff calculator**.
tariffUpdates.scope: Chapter 99 measures that reach Chapter 44 from any country (Section 232 timber and lumber, 2026 Section 301 on 60 economies, Brazil Section 301, Section 338 on Canada, China Section 301 Lists 3 and 4A, Russia; the ended IEEPA and Section 122 duties), and the antidumping and countervailing duty orders and investigations on Chapter 44 goods, which the tariff calculator does not model. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: Chapter 44 base rates: no changes; one line added
changes.detail: All 555 Chapter 44 tariff lines that are in both editions carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition. 4420.19.00.00 (statuettes and other ornaments of non-tropical wood, 3.2%) is not in the 2025 Basic Edition data and is in the current edition.

changes.title: NAFTA panel affirms Commerce on the 2017 softwood lumber CVD investigation
changes.detail: A NAFTA Chapter 19 binational panel affirmed Commerce's second remand redetermination in the review of the original countervailing duty determination on softwood lumber from Canada (USA-CDA-2017-1904-02). The CVD order and current cash-deposit rates are unchanged.

changes.title: Section 232: update on hardwood timber and lumber was due
changes.detail: Proclamation 10976 directed Commerce to update the President by October 1, 2026 on hardwood timber and lumber imports, so the President can decide whether to impose a duty on hardwood lumber and its derivatives. No proclamation had been published by October 13, 2026; hardwood lumber pays no Section 232 duty today.

changes.title: Hardwood and decorative plywood: ITC finds injury; orders pending
changes.detail: The ITC determined that imports of hardwood and decorative plywood (excluding softwood structural plywood) from China, Indonesia and Vietnam injure the U.S. industry, so Commerce will issue antidumping and countervailing duty orders at its final rates. The orders had not been published in the Federal Register by October 13, 2026. The ITC ended the cases on softwood structural plywood as negligible.

changes.title: Section 338: 50% on 154 Canadian wood product lines
changes.detail: Proclamations 11046 and 11048 (July 20, 2026) imposed a 50% duty on products of Canada in the lists of U.S. note 51(b)(1) (9903.03.12) and 51(b)(3) (9903.03.14). In Chapter 44 these cover 154 lines: most plywood, MDF, coniferous veneer and mouldings, particle board other than OSB, wooden doors, charcoal and several wooden articles. Softwood lumber and OSB are not listed. The duty applies even when USMCA is claimed. Proclamation 11056 moved the start from August 19 to August 22, 2026; Proclamations 11064 and 11065 changed the lists from September 15, 2026 without adding or removing Chapter 44 lines.

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 duties on 60 economies; tropical wood exempt
changes.detail: The 10% or 12.5% Section 301 duties on 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) took effect. In Chapter 44 they reach 525 of 556 lines: tropical logs, lumber and veneer are on the general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b)), eleven countries have tropical plywood and mouldings on their note 52(j) lists, and the 15 Section 232 softwood provisions pay that duty instead (note 52(f)). Canadian and Mexican goods entered under USMCA are exempt (notes 52(g)–(h)).

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day 10% surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Brazil Section 301: 25% on most Brazilian wood products
changes.detail: The 25% Section 301 duty on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01) took effect. Tropical logs, lumber, veneer, mouldings and plywood are on its exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03), and Section 232 softwood goods are exempt (note 50(a)(vi)), so it reaches 456 Chapter 44 lines, including Brazilian pine mouldings, doors and plywood.

changes.title: Hardwood and decorative plywood: Commerce final AD/CVD determinations
changes.detail: Commerce found dumping and subsidies on hardwood and decorative plywood. Antidumping: China 187.27% (China-wide entity), Indonesia 18.10% for all others (15.40% to 84.94% for named firms), Vietnam 90.12%. Countervailing: China 88.96%, Indonesia 40.87% for all others (4.22% to 128.66%), Vietnam 47.68% for all others (165.39% for one firm). The goods enter under 35 subheadings of 4412.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still apply.

changes.title: Wood mouldings and millwork from China: orders continued
changes.detail: After five-year sunset reviews, Commerce continued the antidumping and countervailing duty orders on wood mouldings and millwork products from China (goods of 4409, 4412, 4418 and 4421). The China-wide antidumping cash-deposit rate is 220.87%.

changes.title: Softwood lumber from Canada: preliminary 2024 review rates
changes.detail: In the 2024 administrative reviews Commerce preliminarily found AD rates of 16.85% (Canfor), 13.25% (Resolute), 4.77% (West Fraser) and 10.66% for non-examined companies, and CVD rates of 11.70% (Resolute), 15.93% (West Fraser) and 14.17% for non-selected companies. They become cash deposits only when the final results are published; none had been by October 13, 2026.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026. Tropical logs, lumber and veneer (12 subheadings) were on its product exemption list (9903.03.03), Section 232 softwood goods were exempt (9903.03.06), and Canadian and Mexican goods entered under USMCA were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:01 a.m. ET on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Hardwood plywood from China (2018 orders): review results
changes.detail: Commerce completed the 2023 administrative reviews of the 2018 AD and CVD orders on certain hardwood plywood from China. The China-wide antidumping cash-deposit rate is 114.72%. Since July 2023, hardwood plywood completed in Vietnam with Chinese face or back veneers or cores is also covered (circumvention determination, 88 FR 46740).

changes.title: Section 232 wood: increases on cabinets and upholstered furniture moved to 2027
changes.detail: Proclamation 11000 moved the rise from 25% to 50% (kitchen cabinets and vanities) and to 30% (upholstered wooden furniture) from January 1, 2026 to January 1, 2027. These goods are in Chapter 94; the 10% on softwood timber and lumber is unchanged.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29), on every Chapter 44 line. The rate is 0% in 2026.

changes.title: Section 232: 10% on softwood timber and lumber
changes.detail: Proclamation 10976 (September 29, 2025) imposed a 10% duty on softwood timber and lumber (9903.76.01: 106 Chapter 44 lines in 4403, 4406 and 4407.11–4407.19) from every country, with no USMCA exemption, and 25% on kitchen cabinets, vanities and upholstered wooden furniture of Chapter 94. The UK is capped at 10% and the EU and Japan at 15% including the base rate. Goods under these headings are not subject to the reciprocal, Brazil or Canada and Mexico IEEPA duties.

changes.title: Chapter 44 loses its reciprocal-tariff exemption
changes.detail: Proclamation 10976 (clause 12) removed Chapter 44 from Annex II of Executive Order 14257, apart from a few lines on the aligned-partners annex of EO 14346 that are not subject to AD/CVD orders. From then until February 24, 2026, logs, hardwood lumber, panels and plywood other than the Section 232 softwood lines paid the reciprocal tariff.

changes.title: Softwood lumber from Canada: current AD/CVD cash-deposit rates
changes.detail: The 2023 administrative reviews set the cash deposits in force today: antidumping 35.47% (Canfor), 9.65% (West Fraser) and 20.53% for companies not individually examined (amended September 11, 2025); countervailing 12.12% (Canfor), 16.82% (West Fraser) and 14.63% for non-selected companies (August 12, 2025). Exporters never reviewed keep the investigation's 6.04% AD all-others rate. The orders date from January 2018 and were continued in January 2024.

changes.title: Country-specific reciprocal rates take effect
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 replaced the 10% baseline with country-specific reciprocal rates for many partners (for example 15% for the EU, all-inclusive). Wooden articles of 4414–4421 paid them; logs, lumber, panels and plywood stayed exempt under Annex II until October 14, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Brazil: 40% IEEPA duty on Chapter 44
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 added a 40% duty on products of Brazil (9903.01.77). Its Annex I exceptions included only one Chapter 44 subheading, tropical sawn wood of 4407.29.02 (U.S. note 2(x)(iii)), so Brazilian pine lumber, mouldings, doors and plywood paid it. From October 14, 2025 Section 232 softwood goods were exempt. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods from 25% to 35% (9903.01.10). Most Canadian lumber and panels entered under USMCA and did not pay it. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: AD/CVD investigations on hardwood and decorative plywood begin
changes.detail: Commerce initiated antidumping and countervailing duty investigations on hardwood and decorative plywood from China, Indonesia and Vietnam, on a petition by the Coalition for Fair Trade in Hardwood Plywood.

changes.title: China IEEPA duties: reciprocal rate cut to 10%
changes.detail: Chinese wood products paid IEEPA duties on top of Section 301: a fentanyl-related 10% from February 4, 2025 (20% from March 4, back to 10% from November 10, 2025) and, on goods not in Annex II, a reciprocal duty that rose to 125% in April 2025 and was cut to 10% from May 14, 2025. All ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff: lumber and panels exempt, wooden articles covered
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) on products of all countries except Canada and Mexico from April 5, 2025. Annex II (U.S. note 2(v)(iii)) exempted almost all of 4401–4413 (logs, lumber, veneer, mouldings, OSB, MDF, plywood), pending the Section 232 timber investigation; wooden articles of 4414–4421 paid it. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: USMCA goods exempted from the Canada and Mexico duties
changes.detail: From March 7, 2025, goods entered under USMCA were exempt from the IEEPA duties on Canada and Mexico. Non-USMCA wood products kept paying. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duties on products of Canada and Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on goods of Canada (9903.01.10) and Mexico (9903.01.01), in force from March 4, 2025, including lumber, panels and wood products. Ended February 24, 2026.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 44 goods were **$23.21B in 2025**, down 5.3% from $24.51B in 2024 and far below the 2021–2022 peak of about $36B, when lumber prices spiked. **Canada** supplied $10.16B (44%): softwood and other lumber ($4.92B), OSB and particle board ($1.83B), builders' joinery ($1.49B), plywood ($404M) and fiberboard ($370M). **China** ($1.61B, down 25.8%) ships mostly wooden articles, ornaments and kitchenware; **Brazil** ($1.48B) pine mouldings, doors, plywood and lumber; **Vietnam** ($1.38B, up 24.6%), **Indonesia** ($970M) and **Cambodia** ($445M) mainly plywood; **Chile** ($1.14B) plywood, MDF and pine lumber; and **Germany** ($932M), **Sweden** ($453M) and **New Zealand** ($269M) mainly softwood lumber.

By product, softwood lumber leads: S-P-F lumber (4407.13) alone was $3.88B, and the 15 Section 232 softwood provisions together $7.08B (31% of the chapter). OSB (4410.12) fell 23.7% to $1.70B, while plywood with a hardwood face (4412.33) rose 21.2% to $1.69B, as imports shifted to Vietnam and Indonesia, which now face antidumping and countervailing duty cases. Wood charcoal (4402) was $115M, more than half from Mexico.

2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data. The 10% Section 232 duty started on October 14, 2025, so the 2025 figures show only its first weeks; the 2026 Section 301, Brazil and Section 338 duties are not yet visible. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

seo.shortDescription: The total U.S. tariff on lumber, panels, plywood and wood products by country and product group: 10% Section 232 on softwood from everyone, 50% Section 338 on Canadian plywood and MDF, 37.5% on most Brazilian and Chinese wood products, 10% to 12.5% plus base from the other Section 301 economies.

industryAreas.intro:
Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duties for that country, minus any preference, from the current tariff schedule. Antidumping and countervailing duties are **not** included, and they matter here: Canadian softwood lumber carries about 35% in AD/CVD on top of the totals shown, and hardwood plywood from China, and soon from Indonesia and Vietnam, carries much higher rates.

Three things drive the totals. **Softwood lumber, logs and ties** pay the **10% Section 232 duty** from every country, which replaces the Section 301 and Brazil duties on those lines, so the lumber column shows 10% even for Canada with USMCA. **Canada** pays nothing extra on OSB, hardwood lumber and joinery with a USMCA claim, but **50% under Section 338** on most plywood, MDF, doors and mouldings, claim or not. Everyone else pays the **2026 Section 301** duty (10% or 12.5%; EU and Japan in place of lower base rates) on top of base rates up to 8%, with **tropical woods exempt**; **Brazil** adds 25% and **China** 25% (List 3).

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 44: Wood and articles of wood; wood charcoal — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Lumber & Wood Products: Lacey Act, ISPM 15, AD/CVD and Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 44) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Tariff engineering for HTS Chapter 44: classify softwood vs hardwood vs tropical wood correctly, claim USMCA, know your exporter's AD/CVD rate and the order scopes, use drawback (also for Section 232), and meet the Lacey Act, APHIS, ISPM 15, CITES and TSCA formaldehyde rules.
keywords: lacey act form for wood products

tariffEngineering.intro:
The duty on wood depends on three facts: the **species and process** (softwood lumber pays Section 232, tropical wood is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties, hardwood plywood and Chinese mouldings carry AD/CVD), the **origin** (Canada and Mexico with USMCA, China, Brazil, the 60 Section 301 economies) and the **exporter** (AD/CVD rates are company-specific). So the first lever is classifying correctly, ideally with a binding CBP ruling, and the second is knowing which AD/CVD rate and scope apply before you buy.

Wood is also one of the most regulated imports: almost every Chapter 44 good needs a **Lacey Act** plant declaration, logs and lumber must meet **APHIS** rules, wood packaging must be **ISPM 15** treated and marked, listed species need **CITES** permits, composite panels must be **TSCA Title VI** certified, and softwood lumber importers pay the **Softwood Lumber Board** assessment. Each rule and lever links to its regulation.

levers.title: Classify by species, process and shape: softwood, tropical and further-processed wood pay different duties
levers.saves: The 10% Section 232 duty applies only to the 15 softwood provisions in U.S. note 37(b); tropical logs, lumber and veneer are exempt from the 10% or 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duties and Brazil's 25%
levers.document: Species (botanical name, also needed for the Lacey Act declaration), process and dimensions from the mill: for example sawn lumber over 6 mm (4407) vs continuously shaped wood (4409) vs drilled or notched studs (4418), and the face ply species of plywood. A binding ruling under 19 CFR part 177 settles it before import.
levers.caveat: Classification follows what the goods are; mis-declaring species or shape to avoid Section 232 or AD/CVD is fraud. The softwood lumber AD/CVD scope also covers some 4409.10, 4415.20, 4418 and 4421 goods, so moving to another heading does not leave the order.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 37(b), 50(a)(ii) and 52(b)

levers.title: Claim USMCA for Canadian and Mexican wood products
levers.saves: 10% of value: the 2026 Section 301 duty on Canada (9903.05.29) or Mexico (9903.05.55), plus the base rate (up to 8% on plywood and joinery)
levers.appliesTo: Originating goods of Canada and Mexico
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, in the importer's possession when the claim is made (19 CFR 182.12). Rules of origin: General Note 11. Lumber from trees grown and sawn in Canada or Mexico is wholly obtained.
levers.caveat: USMCA does not remove the 10% Section 232 duty on softwood lumber (note 37(a)), the 50% Section 338 duty on the 154 Canadian lines (note 51(a)) or AD/CVD. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 37, 51(a) and 52(g)–(h)
USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Know your exporter's AD/CVD rate and the order scope before you buy
levers.saves: The gap between company rates: on Canadian softwood lumber 26.47% combined for West Fraser vs 35.16% for most exporters and 47.59% for Canfor; on hardwood plywood, from 0% for goods outside the scope to over 270% for China
levers.appliesTo: Softwood lumber from Canada; hardwood plywood from China, Indonesia and Vietnam; wood mouldings and millwork and multilayered wood flooring from China
levers.document: The producer and exporter names on the commercial invoice, matched to Commerce's latest final results; for plywood finished in Vietnam, the certification that no Chinese veneer or core was used (88 FR 46740). When the scope is unclear, ask Commerce for a scope ruling (19 CFR 351.225).
levers.caveat: The written scope decides, not the HTS number. Rates change with each annual review (the 2024 softwood lumber reviews are pending), and the importer must file a non-reimbursement certificate (19 CFR 351.402(f)).

citations.label: 90 FR 44035 and 90 FR 38755 (softwood lumber, current rates)

levers.title: Claim drawback when the wood, or goods made from it, are exported
levers.saves: Generally 99% of the duties paid, including the Section 232 wood duties (Proclamation 10976 clause 14), the Section 301 duties and the base rate, on goods re-exported or used to make exported goods
levers.appliesTo: All lines that paid a duty
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with the import and export records (19 CFR part 191); the claim is generally 99% of the eligible duties (19 CFR 191.51).
levers.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refundable as drawback (19 CFR 191.3(b)(3)). Goods subject to Section 232 admitted to a foreign-trade zone must take privileged foreign status (Proclamation 10976 clause 8).

rules.title: Lacey Act: wood taken or traded in violation of law may not be imported (16 U.S.C. 3372(a)); a plant import declaration with the species, value, quantity and country of harvest is required (16 U.S.C. 3372(f)) and enforced by HTS code. Almost all of Chapter 44 is covered; APHIS planned to add the rest of 4412 and 4413 in phase VII

Logs, lumber and unmanufactured wood: a permit or general permit, plus debarking, heat treatment or fumigation by type and origin (7 CFR 319.40-2, 319.40-3, 319.40-5); wood from Canada enters under general permit; wooden handicrafts from China must be treated and tagged (7 CFR 319.40-5(o))
Wood packaging material (pallets, crates, dunnage) used to ship any goods must be heat-treated or fumigated and carry the ISPM 15 mark, or it is re-exported (7 CFR 319.40-3(b))

CITES-listed timber (for example rosewoods, mahoganies, Spanish cedar, ramin, ebony and agarwood) needs CITES export documents and clears through designated ports; some annotations exempt finished products (50 CFR part 23, 23.92)

Hardwood plywood, particleboard and MDF (and goods made from them) must meet the TSCA Title VI formaldehyde limits, be certified and labeled "TSCA Title VI compliant"; importers must take reasonable precautions and certify TSCA compliance at entry (40 CFR 770.30, 770.45; 19 CFR 12.121)

Softwood lumber of 4407.11–4407.19, 4409.10 and 4418.99.10: importers pay a Softwood Lumber Board assessment of $0.41 per thousand board feet through CBP, except on their first 15 million board feet a year (7 CFR 1217.52, 1217.53); a rule clarifying the import rate takes effect October 22, 2026

Country-of-origin marking: sawed lumber and timbers, utility poles and shingle bundles (other than red cedar) are excepted (Chapter 44 additional U.S. note 2; 19 CFR 134.33); other wood products and the outermost containers must show the origin (19 CFR 134.11, 134.22)
Softwood timber and lumber of the 15 note 37(b) provisions: report 9903.76.01 and pay 10%, also under USMCA; give CBP any information it requires (note 37(k))

groups.note: Wooden tools and handles: Lacey Act declaration and origin marking.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about U.S. tariffs on lumber, plywood and wood products, by country, by product and by HS code. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Softwood timber and lumber pay a 10% Section 232 duty from every country since October 14, 2025, with no USMCA exemption. Canadian softwood lumber also pays AD/CVD cash deposits (35.16% combined for most exporters), about 45% in all.

Most other wood products pay the 2026 Section 301 duty (10% or 12.5%) from the 60 listed economies, with tropical woods exempt; Brazil adds 25%, China pays 25% (List 3) plus 12.5%, and 154 Canadian lines, including most plywood, MDF and doors, pay 50% under Section 338 even with USMCA.

Hardwood plywood carries the heaviest trade remedies: AD/CVD orders on China (and Chinese-core plywood from Vietnam) and final AD/CVD rates on China, Indonesia and Vietnam, with orders pending. The 2025 IEEPA duties ended February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on Canadian lumber?
searchedAs: what is the tariff on canadian lumber
what is the tariff on canadian lumber today
how much is the tariff on lumber from canada
current tariff on lumber from canada
what is the current tariff on canadian softwood lumber
faqs.answer: Canadian softwood lumber (4407.11 to 4407.19) is Free at base but pays the 10% Section 232 duty (9903.76.01) since October 14, 2025, even with a USMCA claim. It also pays antidumping and countervailing duty cash deposits: for most exporters (those not individually examined in the latest reviews) 20.53% AD and 14.63% CVD, so about 45.16% in all. Canfor pays 35.47% AD and 12.12% CVD, West Fraser 9.65% and 16.82%. Preliminary 2024 review rates are lower, but finals are pending.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on lumber right now?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on lumber right now
are there still tariffs on lumber
are there new tariffs on lumber
faqs.answer: Yes. Softwood lumber from every country pays the 10% Section 232 duty. Hardwood lumber pays no Section 232 duty but pays the 2026 Section 301 duty of 10% or 12.5% from the 60 listed economies (Canada and Mexico exempt with USMCA, tropical lumber exempt), 37.5% from Brazil and China, and nothing extra from other countries. Commerce owed the President an update on hardwood lumber by October 1, 2026, which could lead to a duty; none had been proclaimed by October 13, 2026.

faqs.question: What are the softwood lumber duties on Canada?
faqs.answer: Commerce has had antidumping and countervailing duty orders on softwood lumber from Canada since January 2018, continued in January 2024. The cash deposits in force come from the 2023 reviews: AD 20.53% and CVD 14.63% for companies not individually examined, Canfor 35.47% and 12.12%, West Fraser 9.65% and 16.82%. The 2024 reviews preliminarily found 10.66% AD and 14.17% CVD for non-selected companies; they apply only once final. These duties come on top of the 10% Section 232 duty.

faqs.question: What do the Section 232 lumber and wood tariffs cover?
faqs.answer: Proclamation 10976 set three Section 232 duties from October 14, 2025: 10% on softwood timber and lumber (15 provisions of 4403, 4406 and 4407), 25% on upholstered wooden seating and 25% on kitchen cabinets and vanities and their wooden parts (Chapter 94). The UK pays at most 10%, and the EU, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan 15% in all. There is no USMCA exemption. The cabinet and upholstered rates rise to 50% and 30% on January 1, 2027; the 10% on softwood is unchanged.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on kitchen cabinets?
faqs.answer: Wooden kitchen cabinets and vanities are furniture of Chapter 94 (9403.40.90.60, 9403.60.80.93, parts 9403.91.00.80), not Chapter 44. They pay a 25% Section 232 duty (9903.76.03) from most countries, including Canada and Mexico, rising to 50% on January 1, 2027; UK goods pay 10%, and EU, Japanese, South Korean and Taiwanese goods 15% including the base rate. Cabinets that are not wooden enter under 9903.76.04 with no Section 232 duty. Wooden cabinets and vanities from China also carry AD/CVD orders.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on wood products from China?
faqs.answer: Most Chinese wood products pay the base rate (0% to 10.7%) plus 25% under Section 301 List 3 (7.5% on 11 List 4A lines) plus 12.5% under the 2026 Section 301 action: for example 40.8% on other wooden articles of 4421.99.98. Chinese softwood lumber pays 25% plus the 10% Section 232 duty. Hardwood plywood, wood mouldings and millwork, and multilayered wood flooring from China also carry antidumping and countervailing duties, for example 114.72% AD (China-wide) on hardwood plywood.

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on plywood?
faqs.answer: Plywood (4412) has base rates from Free to 8%, plus the 2026 Section 301 duty (12.5% for Vietnam and Chile, 10% for Indonesia, Cambodia and Malaysia; tropical plywood from Indonesia, Cambodia and Malaysia exempt), 37.5% for Brazil and China, and 50% for most Canadian plywood under Section 338. Hardwood and decorative plywood from China, Indonesia and Vietnam has final AD/CVD rates (Vietnam 90.12% AD, 47.68% CVD; Indonesia 18.10% and 40.87%; China 187.27% and 88.96%); the orders were pending on October 13, 2026.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for plywood (4412)?
faqs.answer: Heading 4412 covers plywood, veneered panels and similar laminated wood, split by the material: 4412.10 of bamboo; 4412.31 to 4412.39 plywood of wood veneers only, by the outer ply (4412.31 tropical wood, 4412.33 birch, maple, oak and other listed hardwoods, 4412.34 other hardwoods, 4412.39 softwood on both faces); 4412.41 to 4412.49 LVL; 4412.51 to 4412.59 blockboard; 4412.91 to 4412.99 other. Base rates run from Free (for example birch-faced plywood of 4412.33.06) to 8%.

faqs.question: What is HS code 4407?
faqs.answer: 4407 is wood sawn or chipped lengthwise, sliced or peeled, over 6 mm thick, that is, lumber: 4407.11 pine, 4407.12 fir and spruce, 4407.13 S-P-F, 4407.14 hem-fir, 4407.19 other softwood; 4407.21 to 4407.29 tropical woods; 4407.91 to 4407.99 other hardwoods such as oak, beech, maple, cherry, ash and birch. All are Free at base; 4407.11 to 4407.19 pay the 10% Section 232 duty. 4407.13 was the largest Chapter 44 import in 2025 ($3.88B).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for wooden pallets and crates?
faqs.answer: Heading 4415: 4415.10 cases, boxes, crates, drums and cable drums (Free, except other cases of 4415.10.90 at 10.7%), and 4415.20 pallets, box pallets and pallet collars (Free for harvest containers of 4415.20.40, 10.7% for other pallets of 4415.20.80). Wood packaging used to ship goods, whether imported as cargo or in use, must be heat-treated or fumigated and carry the ISPM 15 mark (7 CFR 319.40-3(b)).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for charcoal?
faqs.answer: Wood charcoal, including lump and briquette charcoal, is heading 4402: 4402.10 of bamboo, 4402.20 of shell or nut (coconut shell), and 4402.90 other. All are Free at base. Activated charcoal is heading 3802, and charcoal grills are classified elsewhere. Canadian charcoal of 4402.90 pays 50% under Section 338. Mexico supplied more than half of the $115M imported in 2025.

faqs.question: What does the Lacey Act require for wood imports?
searchedAs: lacey act form for wood products
faqs.answer: The Lacey Act bans importing wood taken or traded in violation of U.S. or foreign law, and requires a plant import declaration with each entry: the scientific name of each species, the value, the quantity and the country of harvest (16 U.S.C. 3372(f)). APHIS enforces it by HTS code; almost all of Chapter 44 is covered. Packaging used only to carry other goods is exempt.

faqs.question: What are the ISPM 15 requirements for wood packaging?
faqs.answer: Under 7 CFR 319.40-3(b), wood pallets, crates and dunnage entering the U.S. must be heat-treated or fumigated with methyl bromide and marked, preferably on two opposite sides, with the IPPC mark showing the country code, the producer number and the treatment (HT or MB). Unmarked wood packaging can be ordered re-exported at the port of arrival.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import lumber and wood products from?
searchedAs: lumber imports from canada to us
faqs.answer: Mostly Canada: $10.16B, or 44% of the $23.21B of Chapter 44 goods imported in 2025, led by lumber ($4.92B) and OSB ($1.83B). Next come China ($1.61B), Brazil ($1.48B), Vietnam ($1.38B), Chile ($1.14B), Indonesia ($970M), Germany ($932M), Mexico ($681M), Sweden ($453M) and Cambodia ($445M). Imports fell 5.3% from 2024.

faqs.question: What does HTS Chapter 44 cover?
searchedAs: wood and articles of wood wood charcoal hs code
faqs.answer: HTS Chapter 44, "Wood and articles of wood; wood charcoal", is in Section IX with cork (Chapter 45) and basketware (Chapter 46). It has 21 headings (4401 to 4421) and 556 ten-digit U.S. lines: fuel wood and pellets, charcoal, logs, lumber, veneer, mouldings, OSB, MDF, plywood, frames, pallets, barrels, joinery, kitchenware and other wooden articles. Wooden furniture is in Chapter 94.
